questions.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
questions.problem:
Given that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡3t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡3t$ for $s>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{8\operatorname{cos}⁡3t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡3t} & =L{8\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}+L{-5\operatorname{sin}⁡3t} \\  & =8L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}-5L{\operatorname{sin}⁡3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{sin}⁡3t} & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =8L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}-5L{\operatorname{sin}⁡3t} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}-5\cdot \frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9} \\  & =\frac{8s}{{s}^{2}+9}-\frac{15}{{s}^{2}+9} \\  & =\frac{8s-15}{{s}^{2}+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t$ for $s>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+L{3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+3\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{3s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{3s+2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)=\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-5t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-5t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5},\,s>5 \\ L{{e}^{-5t}} & =\frac{1}{s+5},\,s>-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-5}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+5} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-5}-\frac{1}{s+5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+5)-(s-5)}{(s-5)(s+5)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{10}{{s}^{2}-25}) \\  & =\frac{5}{{s}^{2}-25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{5t}}$ is defined for $s\in (5,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-5t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-5,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t)}$ is defined for

$$
(5,\infty )\cap (-5,\infty )=(5,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions
questions.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the cosine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)=\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}+{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}+{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+4\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+4\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}+\frac{1}{s+4\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+4\text{i})+(s-4\text{i})}{(s-4\text{i})(s+4\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+16}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
questions.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t)$ for $s>6.$
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t)} & =L{2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t)} \\  & =2L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-36},\,s>6 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t)} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-36},\,s>6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =2L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)}+L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t)} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}-36}+\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-36} \\  & =\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-36}+\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-36} \\  & =\frac{2s+6}{{s}^{2}-36}.\end{aligned}
$$
